text:
Open Desk: this space is yours.

Post something you made this week in the replies. Finished or not, paid or not, sure about it or not. We'll look at every one.

Nobody walks into a shop because the logo was nice.

They come in because they remember you, and they come back because you felt like you meant it. A logo helps with the remembering. The rest is how you speak, how you behave, and what you'd never do. That's the bigger job.

The first idea in the room is the one any studio would have had. It feels obvious because it's obvious to everyone, your competitors included.

So we keep drawing. Somewhere around the sixth or seventh, the ideas stop being safe and start being yours.

AI can hand you a hundred logos before your tea goes cold. That part is solved.

What it can't do is know which one belongs to your business, why, and what you'll have to give up to choose it. Choosing is the job. It always was.

In Slemani the tea arrives before the agenda does, and we've stopped fighting it.

The ten minutes of small talk show you how someone talks about their business when they're not presenting it. That's usually the version worth designing for.

Kurdish and Arabic readers start on the right.

Layouts copied from English templates put the headline on the left, so it gets read last. Before anything else, we check where the eye actually lands.

Most About Us pages read like the paragraph we crossed out. Dynamic, customer-focused, committed to excellence. Every business could sign it, so no customer remembers it.

Find the one sentence only you could say. Then put it everywhere.

For years the safe brief in this region was “make it look like Dubai.” Glass, gold, a font from a hotel lobby.

It never quite fit, because it was always somewhere else. The brands people remember here will look like where they're from: our streets, our script, our sense of humour.

Before a first meeting with us, bring three things:

What you sell, in one line.
Who you most need to win.
What you'd never do, even for money.

The third one tells us the most. We'll bring the tea. hello@33studio.org

A teacher. An older brother. A cartoon on TV. A grandmother who drew patterns for embroidery.

Someone handed you a pencil and didn't take it back. Tag them below. They almost never hear that it mattered.

Your shop closes. Your sign doesn't.

It's still out there at midnight, telling the street what you are to people who've never been inside. It's the hardest-working thing you own, and often the least designed. We design signs and storefronts that earn the night shift. 33studio.org
